commentary.bottom_line: Twenty-two guidance documents, frameworks, commentaries, and one state statute endorse legal review of AI systems and data contracts for privacy compliance, but no supplied study tests whether this review prevents privacy violations. The recommendation rests on legal obligation and expert consensus rather than on measured outcomes.

perspectives.view: No study in the supplied set tests the practice, and no study documents the hazard's frequency or severity. The support consists of 22 endorsements, most of them guidance and commentary. Under GRADE conventions this yields no direct evidence. The consistency of the endorsements reflects agreement on a legal duty, and agreement of that kind cannot be read as a measured effect.

Parts of this recommendation restate existing law. HIPAA already applies to covered entities and their business associates. Texas SB 1188 requires reasonable administrative, physical, and technical safeguards for electronic health record information. Compliance review is therefore a legal requirement in these settings whatever the evidence base shows. Tracking legal change matters because state AI and privacy statutes continue to change.

Reviewing every AI system and its data contracts requires legal and privacy staff time. The volume of that work grows with the number of vendors and with the jurisdictions whose law applies. No supplied study reports what this review costs, how long it takes, or how many staff it needs. Organizations will have to estimate the burden from their own contract inventories.

commentary.research_gap: No study measures whether structured legal review of AI systems and data contracts reduces privacy incidents, contract breaches, or regulatory findings. No study compares review models, such as review at procurement alone versus periodic re-review as laws change. No study reports the staffing burden of each approach.
commentary.underserved_note: No supplied study tested the practice in any population, including Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Safety-net organizations may have fewer legal staff to carry out this review. Whether privacy protections reach these patients equally therefore cannot be assessed from the supplied evidence.
